43	## 2. Statements
44	
45	### 2.1 File structure
46	
47	A statement is a text file in UTF-8. A leading byte order mark is ignored. The file has three parts, in this order:
48	
49	1. Header lines. Each starts with `#` and has the form `#key: value`. Keys are case-insensitive and are stored in lower case; values are stripped of surrounding spaces.
50	2. The column line, which names the columns in the order the rows use them. Blank lines between the header and the column line are ignored.
51	3. Rows. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored here too; such a `#` line is a comment, not a header.
52	
53	Line numbers in error messages are one-based and count every physical line of the file, including header lines and blank lines.
54	
55	### 2.2 Header keys
56	
57	| Key | Required | Meaning |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| `account` | yes | Name of the account the statement belongs to. Used as the report name. |
60	| `currency` | yes | ISO 4217 code of the statement currency (case-insensitive). |
61	| `dialect` | no | Name of a dialect from the dialect table (section 3). |
62	| `delimiter` | no | Field separator (section 3.2). |
63	| `decimal` | no | Decimal mark of amounts: `.` or `,`. |
64	| `date_order` | no | `ymd`, `dmy` or `mdy` (section 5.1). |
65	| `jurisdiction` | no | Tax jurisdiction code (section 10). Empty means the statement is not taxed. |
66	| `fiscal_start` | no | Month number 1 to 12 in which the account's fiscal year starts (section 5.3). |
67	| `opened` | no | Informational; not interpreted. |
68	| `note` | no | Informational; not interpreted. |
69	
70	An unknown key, a key that appears twice, or a missing required key is a `HeaderError`.
71	
72	### 2.3 Columns
73	
74	The required columns are `id`, `date`, `description` and `amount`. The optional columns are `reverses`, `category` and `tax`. Column names are case-insensitive, and columns may appear in any order. An unknown column name, a repeated name or a missing required column is a `FormatError` on the column line.
75	
76	Every row must have exactly as many fields as the column line. Fields are stripped of surrounding spaces. Quoting follows the usual CSV rules, so a field that contains the delimiter is written in double quotes.
77	
78	| Column | Meaning |
79	|---|---|
80	| `id` | Entry id, unique within the statement. Ids are compared exactly as written (case-sensitive). |
81	| `date` | Posting date, in the statement's date order. |
82	| `description` | Free text. |
83	| `amount` | Signed amount in the statement currency (section 4). Positive amounts increase the account, negative amounts decrease it. |
84	| `reverses` | Id of the entry this row cancels, or empty (section 8). |
85	| `category` | Dotted category path, stored in lower case, or empty (section 9). |
86	| `tax` | Tax code `S`, `R`, `Z` or `E`, stored in upper case, or empty (section 10). |
87	
88	An empty id, an id used twice (`DuplicateEntry`) and an entry that reverses itself are errors.
89	
90	### 2.4 Other formats
91	
92	`ledger.parse.importers` reads two more formats into the same `Statement`: JSON lines (`.jsonl`) and fixed-width text (`.txt`). Both are converted to CSV text first, so every rule in this note applies to them unchanged. In both formats amounts are strings written in the statement's layout. A `delimiter` header key in these formats is ignored, because the converted text is always comma-delimited.
93	
94	### 2.5 Writing statements
95	
96	`ledger.parse.writer.write_statement` writes a statement so that it reads back to the same entries. It writes the dialect name when the statement has one and also every layout key explicitly, so the written file does not depend on the dialect table. Amounts are written without group separators and with a leading minus for negatives.
97	
98	## 3. Dialects and layout
99	
100	### 3.1 What a layout is
101	
102	The layout of a statement is the set of four values that decide how its body is read: `delimiter`, `decimal`, `date_order` and `jurisdiction`. `Statement.layout` holds the layout a statement was read with, and `ledger check` prints it.
103	
104	### 3.2 Delimiter values
105	
106	A `delimiter` value is either a name (`comma`, `semicolon`, `pipe`, `tab`, case-insensitive) or a single character that is not a letter, a digit, a quote or `#`. A tab can only be given by name.
107	
108	### 3.3 Dialects
109	
110	A dialect records the layout one sender uses for all its statements, so that a header can name the sender (`#dialect: northgate`) instead of spelling each value out. Dialect names are case-insensitive. The table is in `ledger.parse._dialect_table`; an unknown name is `UnknownDialect`.
111	
112	### 3.4 Which value wins
113	
114	Each layout key takes its value from the first of these sources that has one:
115	
116	1. the statement's own header line for that key;
117	2. the dialect named by the statement's `dialect` header;
118	3. the base layout: delimiter `,`, decimal `.`, date order `ymd`, no jurisdiction.
119	
120	A header line therefore always wins over the dialect. This is what lets one sender's statement deviate from its usual layout (an export made with a different setting, or an account held in another jurisdiction) without a new dialect. A dialect only fills the keys the header leaves out.
121	
122	Example: the `northgate` dialect is semicolon-delimited with a `,` decimal mark, `dmy` dates and jurisdiction `ARD`. A statement with the header lines below is read with delimiter `,`, decimal `.`, `ymd` dates and jurisdiction `ARD`:
123	
124	    #account: cross-month
125	    #currency: EUR
126	    #dialect: northgate
127	    #delimiter: comma
128	    #decimal: .
129	    #date_order: ymd
130	
131	### 3.5 Checks on a layout
132	
133	`decimal` must be `.` or `,`; `date_order` must be one of the three orders. The delimiter and the decimal mark must differ, except that a `,` delimiter with a `,` decimal mark is allowed because such amounts are quoted. Violations are `HeaderError`.
134	
135	### 3.6 Guessing
136	
137	`ledger.parse.sniff` guesses a layout from a file's body and `ledger check --guess` compares the guess with the layout the file is read with. The guess is advisory: reading always follows section 3.4, never the guess.
138	
139	## 4. Amounts
140	
141	### 4.1 Minor units
142	
143	Amounts are stored as integers in minor units of their currency. The number of minor-unit digits is the currency's exponent from `ledger.core._currency_table`: 2 for most currencies, 0 for currencies such as JPY or KRW, 3 for currencies such as KWD, BHD or TND. So `12.34` EUR is 1234, `1500` JPY is 1500 and `1.5` KWD is 1500.
144	
145	### 4.2 Accepted forms
146	
147	An amount consists of, in order:
148	
149	- an optional sign: a leading `-` or `+`, or surrounding parentheses for a negative amount (`(7.25)` is -725). Spaces inside the parentheses are allowed. A sign inside parentheses, and unbalanced parentheses, are errors;
150	- a whole part of digits, optionally with group separators;
151	- optionally, the decimal mark followed by one or more digits, at most as many as the currency's exponent. Fewer digits are padded: `2450.5` is 245050 cents.
152	
153	The decimal mark is the statement's `decimal` value. The group separator is `,` when the decimal mark is `.`, and `.` when the decimal mark is `,`. A space is also accepted as a group separator. Group separators may only appear in the whole part, and must split it into groups of three digits after a first group of one to three digits (`1,234,567` is fine, `12,34` is not).
154	
155	Anything else is a `FormatError`: an empty amount, more fraction digits than the exponent allows (`1.234` for EUR, `1.5` for JPY), a decimal mark without digits after it, more than one decimal mark, letters, or a bare sign.
156	
157	### 4.3 Display
158	
159	Formatting goes the other way (`ledger.core.money.format_amount`): the whole part, the decimal mark and exactly `exponent` fraction digits, with an optional group separator every three digits. A negative amount is written with a single leading minus sign before its digits and is otherwise written exactly like the positive amount of the same size: -50 cents is `-0.50`, -123456 cents is `-1,234.56` with `,` groups. Zero is never negative. Section 12 says which formats use which separators.
160	
161	## 5. Dates, months and fiscal periods
162	
163	### 5.1 Date orders
164	
165	| Order | Example | Separators |
166	|---|---|---|
167	| `ymd` | `2026-01-31` | `-` |
168	| `dmy` | `31/01/2026`, `31.01.2026` | `/` or `.` |
169	| `mdy` | `01/31/2026` | `/` |
170	
171	Years have four digits; day and month have one or two. A date that does not exist (`2026-02-30`) or does not match the order is a `FormatError`.
172	
173	### 5.2 Month keys
174	
175	A month key is `YYYY-MM`. Month keys sort correctly as strings. `iter_months(first, last)` includes both ends; `months_between(start, stop)` is half-open and excludes `stop`. A range written in a data file (rate files, section 6.1) always includes both of its end months.
176	
177	### 5.3 Fiscal years
178	
179	A fiscal year starts on the first day of the account's `fiscal_start` month (1 when absent) and is named after the calendar year in which it ends. With `fiscal_start` 4, April 2025 to March 2026 is FY2026. Quarters are numbered from the start of the fiscal year: with `fiscal_start` 4, January 2026 is in FY2026-Q4.
180	
181	### 5.4 Weeks and business days
182	
183	Weeks follow ISO 8601 (`ledger.periods.weeks`). A business day is a Monday to Friday that is not a public holiday of the statement's jurisdiction (`ledger.periods._holiday_table`); a statement without a jurisdiction only skips weekends. Business days are used by the aging report only.
184	
185	## 6. Exchange rates
186	
187	### 6.1 Rate files
188	
189	A rate file is a CSV file with the columns `currency`, `from`, `to` and `rate`, in that order. Lines starting with `#` and blank lines are ignored. Each row says that, in every month from `from` to `to` (both included), one major unit of `currency` was worth `rate` US dollars. A row whose `from` and `to` are the same month covers exactly that month.
190	
191	Rules:
192	
193	- `rate` is a positive decimal written with digits and at most one `.`, with at most 8 decimal places. Exponent notation, signs and group separators are rejected.
194	- `from` and `to` are month keys and `to` is not before `from`.
195	- The base currency has no rows; a USD row is an error.
196	- Two rows that cover the same currency and month are a `RateConflict`, whether they are in one file or in two files loaded together.
197	
198	The table built from a rate file (`RateTable`) holds exactly the months the rows cover, one entry per currency and month.
199	
200	### 6.2 Which rate applies to a month
201	
202	The rate for a currency in a month is chosen as follows:
203	
204	1. If the rate table lists the month, that rate is used.
205	2. Otherwise the most recent earlier month that the table lists is used, provided it is at most three months before the month in question (`MAX_LOOKBACK`). The rate is then said to be carried from that month.
206	3. Otherwise there is no rate, and `MissingRate` is raised.
207	
208	A later month's rate is never used, not even when it is closer than the nearest earlier one: it was not known at the time of the entry. Examples, with rates listed for January to March and for May:
209	
210	| Month | Rate used |
211	|---|---|
212	| March | March |
213	| April | March (carried, one month back) |
214	| May | May |
215	| December of the year before | none: `MissingRate`, even though January is only one month later |
216	
217	With rates listed only for January, April is carried from January (three months back) and May has no rate.
218	
219	The base currency always has the rate 1 in every month.
220	
221	### 6.3 Cross rates
222	
223	The cross rate from currency A to currency B in a month is rate(A) / rate(B), each chosen as in 6.2, rounded to 6 decimal places with the rule of section 7.2. Converting an amount between two non-base currencies goes through the base currency exactly, and only the result is rounded to whole minor units of B.
224	
225	## 7. Conversion and rounding
226	
227	### 7.1 Converting one entry
228	
229	An amount of `m` minor units of a currency with exponent `e`, at rate `r`, is worth exactly `m * r * 10^(2 - e)` US cents. This value is computed with exact decimal arithmetic (Python `Decimal`), never with binary floats.
230	
231	Each entry is converted on its own and rounded to whole cents (7.2) before it is added to anything. Every total in every report (a month, a category, a tax code, a trial balance row, a report total) is a sum of rounded entry values. Totals are never rounded again, and an exact sum is never rounded as a whole. For example, two entries of 41.00 EUR at 1.0825 are each 4438.25 cents exactly; each rounds to 4438, and their month total is 8876, not the 8877 that rounding their exact sum 8876.5 would give.
232	
233	### 7.2 The rounding rule
234	
235	All rounding in the package rounds to the nearest integer, and a value exactly halfway between two integers is rounded away from zero:
236	
237	| Exact value | Rounded |
238	|---|---|
239	| 216.5 | 217 |
240	| -216.5 | -217 |
241	| 2.5 | 3 |
242	| 3.5 | 4 |
243	| -0.5 | -1 |
244	| 10.49 | 10 |
245	
246	The same rule applies when rounding to decimal places (cross rates, percentages, statistics): 1.23455 to four places is 1.2346. Rounding half to even ("banker's rounding") is not used anywhere, because it does not match the rounding the senders use on their own statements.
247	
248	`ledger.core.rounding.round_half_away` implements this rule and every other module rounds through it (or through `round_to`, which uses the same rule).
249	
250	### 7.3 Allocation
251	
252	`allocate(total, weights)` splits an integer amount in proportion to weights with the largest remainder method; the shares always add up to the total. Remainders go one unit at a time to the largest fractional parts, earlier positions first on ties. Negative totals are allocated as their absolute value and negated.
253	
254	## 8. Reversals
255	
256	### 8.1 What a reversal is
257	
258	An entry whose `reverses` column names another entry of the same statement cancels that entry. The entry it names is called the original.
259	
260	### 8.2 Checks
261	
262	A reversal must satisfy all of these, or `UnmatchedReversal` is raised:
263	
264	- the original exists in the same statement;
265	- the original is itself a regular entry, not a reversal;
266	- the reversal's amount is exactly the negated amount of the original;
267	- the reversal is not dated before the original;
268	- no other reversal already cancels the same original.
269	
270	### 8.3 Booking period and valuation
271	
272	A reversal does not create an event of its own in the reports; it undoes the original. Therefore:
273	
274	- it is booked in the period (month) of the original entry, not in the month in which it was posted;
275	- it is valued as of the original entry's date: it is converted at the rate that applies to the original's month (section 6.2), and when it is taxed, the tax rule in force on the original's date applies (section 10.2).
276	
277	Both dates come from the original. In `ledger.book.reversals`, a `Booking` carries a `period_date` and a `valuation_date`; for a regular entry both are its own date, and for a reversal both are the original's date. A matched pair therefore nets to exactly zero in every report, in every currency and for tax, even when the reversal is posted in a later month whose exchange rate or tax rate differs.
278	
279	Example: an entry of -150.40 EUR dated 20 January and its reversal dated 3 February both belong to January and are both converted at January's rate. The February report does not show either of them.
280	
281	### 8.4 Reversals elsewhere
282	
283	Splits (13.2) split a reversal with the same weights as its original, part by part. The audit (`ledger audit`) reports reversals posted more than 60 days after their original; this is informational only.
284	
285	## 9. Categories and accounts
286	
287	### 9.1 Resolution
288	
289	The chart of accounts (`ledger.book._chart`) maps categories to account codes. A category is a dotted path such as `travel.rail.season`. An entry's category is resolved to the account of the longest listed prefix of its path: `travel.rail.night` uses the account of `travel.rail` when only that is listed, and `travel.bus` uses the account of `travel`. Categories are compared in lower case.
290	
291	An empty category goes to the suspense account `9990`. A non-empty category with no listed prefix, or with an empty segment (`travel..rail`), is `UnknownCategory`.
292	
293	### 9.2 Suggestions and rules
294	
295	`ledger suggest` proposes categories for entries without one, from the merchant table. Suggestions are never applied by the reports. A rules file (`ledger.book.rules`) can assign categories to uncategorized entries before booking, when a caller applies it explicitly; reading a statement never applies rules.
296	
297	## 10. Tax
298	
299	### 10.1 Codes and jurisdictions
300	
301	Tax codes are `S` (standard), `R` (reduced), `Z` (zero rated) and `E` (exempt). Each jurisdiction in `ledger.tax._rule_table` has, per code, a list of rules: a date from which a rate applies, and the rate. Rates in the table are written as fractions (`0.095`) or percentages (`9.5%`).
302	
303	A statement is taxed in its layout's jurisdiction. An entry with a tax code in a statement without a jurisdiction, an unknown jurisdiction, an unknown code, or a date before the code's first rule is `UnknownTaxCode`. Entries without a tax code are not part of tax reports.
304	
305	### 10.2 Which rule applies
306	
307	The rule that applies on a day is the rule of the entry's code with the latest effective date that is on or before that day. A rule takes effect on its effective date itself: a rate that applies from 1 March 2026 applies to an entry valued on 1 March 2026, and the previous rate applies to an entry valued on 28 February 2026.
308	
309	The day is the entry's valuation date (section 8.3): its own date for a regular entry, the original's date for a reversal.
310	
311	### 10.3 Tax portion
312	
313	Statement amounts include tax. For an entry, the gross amount G is its converted and rounded value in US cents (section 7.1). With rate r, the tax portion is G * r / (1 + r) rounded with the rule of 7.2, and the net amount is G minus the tax portion. Tax portions are computed per entry and then added up; they are never computed from a total.
314	
315	Because the rounding rule is symmetric, the tax of a reversal is exactly the negated tax of its original.
316	
317	### 10.4 Returns and schedules
318	
319	A quarterly return (`ledger return`) adds the per-entry tax lines of one jurisdiction's statements by calendar quarter of their valuation dates. `ledger schedule` prints a jurisdiction's rules; each rule's "until" date is the effective date of the next rule of the same code, and the rule no longer applies on that date.
320	
321	## 11. Reports
322	
323	### 11.1 Monthly report
324	
325	`build_monthly` returns:
326	
327	    {"account": "...", "currency": "EUR", "base": "USD",
328	     "months": {"2026-01": -12345, ...}, "total": -12345}
329	
330	`months` holds, for each booking period that has at least one entry, the sum of the rounded values of the entries booked in it (sections 7.1 and 8.3), in calendar order. A month whose entries cancel out is listed with 0. `total` is the sum of the month values.
331	
332	### 11.2 Tax report
333	
334	`build_vat` returns, per tax code used by the statement, the sums of the per-entry gross, net and tax amounts (section 10.3), plus `total_tax`, the sum of the tax amounts. Codes are listed in alphabetical order. A statement without taxed entries has an empty `codes` mapping.
335	
336	### 11.3 Balances, summaries and comparisons
337	
338	- Balances list every month from the first to the last month of a monthly report, months without entries included, with the movement and the closing balance.
339	- Fiscal summaries add month values by fiscal quarter and fiscal year (section 5.3).
340	- Month-over-month and year-over-year comparisons give percentages rounded to one decimal with the rule of 7.2, written with a sign (`+12.5%`). A change from zero is `new`.
341	
342	### 11.4 Trial balance and account matrix
343	
344	The trial balance and the account-by-month matrix are built from journal postings. A posting is one entry, booked and valued as in sections 7 and 8, assigned to the account of its category. An account's net is the sum of its postings; a positive net is shown as a debit and a negative net, as a positive number, as a credit.
345	
346	### 11.5 Other reports
347	
348	- Aging lists open receivables (positive regular entries in a `receivable` account that no reversal cancels) by business days outstanding, in buckets 0-20, 21-40, 41-60 and 61+. Amounts stay in the statement currency.
349	- Revaluation compares, at each month end, the book value (sum of posted rounded values) with the running balance converted once at that month's rate.
350	- Reconciliation compares sender-reported closing balances with the sum of entries by posting date. It deliberately ignores booking periods, because the sender does not know them.
351	- Budgets compare planned and actual account totals by month.
352	
353	## 12. Rendering
354	
355	All renderers take the report dicts of section 11 and show amounts in major units of US dollars with two decimals.
356	
357	| Format | Decimal mark | Group separator | Negative amounts | Example |
358	|---|---|---|---|---|
359	| text | `.` | `,` | leading minus | `-1,234.56` |
360	| CSV | `.` | none | leading minus | `-1234.56` |
361	| Markdown | `.` | `,` | leading minus | `-1,234.56` |
362	| HTML | `.` | `,` | leading minus, cell class `neg` | `-1,234.56` |
363	| JSON | not applicable | not applicable | integer cents | `-123456` |
364	
365	All of them use `ledger.core.money.format_amount`, whose output is defined in section 4.3; a renderer never formats amounts on its own. Small negative amounts keep their sign: -50 cents is `-0.50` in text, CSV, Markdown and HTML alike.
366	
367	The accounting style (`format_accounting`) puts negative amounts in parentheses. It is only used where a caller asks for it explicitly; no report format uses it.
368	
369	Text output: a title line, then a table whose columns are separated by two spaces, text left-aligned and amounts right-aligned, with trailing spaces removed from every line. The monthly report's last row is `total`.
370	
371	CSV output: a header row, then one row per line of the report, lines ending with `\n`, fields quoted only when needed.
372	
373	Markdown output: a `###` title, a blank line, and a pipe table whose amount columns are right-aligned (`---:`); the total row's label is bold.
374	
375	JSON output: keys sorted, two-space indentation, a final newline.
376	
377	## 13. Auxiliary files
378	
379	### 13.1 Budgets
380	
381	CSV with columns `account`, `month`, `amount`; amounts in US dollars with a `.` decimal mark, negative for spending. One line per account and month.
382	
383	### 13.2 Splits
384	
385	CSV with columns `id`, `category`, `weight`. An entry named in the file is replaced by one part per line, sharing its amount with `allocate` (section 7.3). Part ids get the suffix `/1`, `/2`, ... in file order.
386	
387	### 13.3 Closing files
388	
389	One month key per line; `#` starts a comment. `late_entries` lists the entries booked into a closed month although they were posted after that month ended (for instance a reversal posted in February of an entry from a closed January).
390	
391	### 13.4 Balance files
392	
393	CSV with columns `month` and `closing`; amounts in the statement currency with a `.` decimal mark.
394	
395	### 13.5 Workspace file
396	
397	`ledger.toml` may set `[ledger] rates`, `statements` and `pattern`, and `[report] format`. Unknown sections or keys are errors.
398	
399	## 14. Command line
400	
401	`python -m ledger <command>` runs from the workspace directory. Rates come from `--rates`, else from the `LEDGER_RATES` environment variable, else from `data/rates.csv` under the current directory. Output goes to standard output; errors go to standard error as `ledger: <ErrorType>: <message>` with exit status 2. `python -m ledger --help` and `python -m ledger <command> --help` list the commands and options.
402	
403	### 14.1 Reports of one statement
404	
405	| Command | Output |
406	|---|---|
407	| `report STATEMENT [--format F] [--detail]` | Monthly report (11.1). With `--detail`, one CSV line per entry: id, posting date, booking period, the month whose rate was used, and the value in US dollars. |
408	| `vat STATEMENT [--format F]` | Tax report (11.2). |
409	| `balances STATEMENT [--format F]` | Running balances (11.3). |
410	| `summary STATEMENT [--format F]` | Fiscal quarters and years (11.3). |
411	| `explain STATEMENT ID` | How one entry is read, booked, valued and taxed, one stage per line. |
412	| `revalue STATEMENT` | Month-end revaluation (11.5), as JSON. |
413	| `aging STATEMENT DATE` | Open receivables on DATE (11.5). |
414	| `audit STATEMENT` | Findings worth a second look; they never stop a report. |
415	| `suggest STATEMENT` | Category suggestions for uncategorized entries (9.2). |
416	| `outlook STATEMENT [--months N]` | Recurring payments projected forward, in the statement currency. |
417	
418	`--format` is one of `text`, `csv`, `markdown` and `json` (section 12); `text` when absent.
419	
420	### 14.2 Several statements
421	
422	| Command | Output |
423	|---|---|
424	| `trial STATEMENT... [--period MONTH]` | Trial balance (11.4), optionally for one booking period. |
425	| `matrix STATEMENT...` | Account-by-month matrix (11.4), as JSON. |
426	| `transfers STATEMENT...` | Pairs of cash entries in different statements that cancel within a tolerance and lie at most three days apart. |
427	| `return STATEMENT...` | Quarterly tax return of one jurisdiction (10.4), as JSON. |
428	| `export STATEMENT...` | Postings as plain-text double-entry transactions. |
429	| `budget BUDGET STATEMENT...` | Budget against actual (13.1), as CSV. |
430	| `overview STATEMENT...` | One line per statement: currency, dialect, entries, reversals, date range. |
431	
432	### 14.3 Files and tables
433	
434	| Command | Output |
435	|---|---|
436	| `check STATEMENT... [--guess]` | One line per statement: `ok` with the layout it was read with, or `FAIL` with the first problem. Exit status 1 when any statement fails. With `--guess`, also compares each file's body with that layout (3.6). |
437	| `validate STATEMENT` | Every row-level problem of a statement, not only the first. |
438	| `diff OLD NEW` | Entries added, removed or changed between two versions of a statement, and layout changes. |
439	| `rate CURRENCY MONTH` | The rate that applies (6.2) and the month it comes from. |
440	| `rates` | Per currency: listed range, missing months, low, high, mean and spread of the rates. |
441	| `dialects [NAME]` | The dialect table, or one dialect's layout. |
442	| `schedule JURISDICTION` | Every tax rule of a jurisdiction with the date it ends (10.4). |
443	
444	## 15. Errors
445	
446	Every error the package raises on purpose is a `LedgerError`. `FormatError` (and its subclass `HeaderError`) carry the file and one-based line when they come from a file, and show them as `path line N: message`. Errors are raised, never logged and skipped: a statement either reads completely or not at all.
447	
448	## 16. Worked examples
449	
450	The examples use these rates: EUR 1.0825 for January to March 2026 (one row), EUR 1.0910 for May and June 2026, and nothing for April.
451	
452	### 16.1 One entry from file to report
453	
454	A row `b3,2026-02-02,Rail pass,-84,,travel.rail.season,R` in a EUR statement with jurisdiction ARD:
455	
456	1. Amount: `-84` has no fraction, so it is -8400 minor units (4.2).
457	2. Booking: a regular entry, so period and valuation date are its own date, 2 February 2026 (8.3).
458	3. Rate: February is listed, rate 1.0825 (6.2).
459	4. Conversion: -8400 * 1.0825 = -9093.0000 cents exactly, -9093 after rounding (7.1).
460	5. Account: `travel.rail.season` is listed, account 5211 (9.1).
461	6. Tax: code R in ARD on 2 February 2026; the reduced rule in force on that day is 9.5% from 15 October 2025 (10.2). Tax portion -9093 * 0.095 / 1.095 = -788.89..., rounded -789; net -8304 (10.3).
462	
463	### 16.2 A month without a listed rate
464	
465	An entry of 100.00 EUR dated 10 April 2026 uses March's rate, 1.0825, carried one month (6.2): 10825 cents. It does not use May's rate, although May is listed and equally close. An entry dated 10 December 2025 has no rate at all, because no earlier month is listed: `MissingRate`.
466	
467	### 16.3 A reversal posted in a later month
468	
469	Entry x2 of -150.40 EUR on 20 January 2026 is reversed by x3, +150.40 EUR on 3 February 2026. Both are booked in January and both are converted at January's rate: -16281 and +16281 cents. January's total includes both; February's does not include x3. If January and February had different rates, x3 would still use January's. If the tax rate changed on 1 February, x3 would still be taxed at the rate in force on 20 January.
470	
471	### 16.4 Rounding a month
472	
473	A EUR statement with two entries of 41.00 in February at 1.0825: each is 4438.25 cents exactly and 4438 rounded. February's total is 8876. Rounding the exact sum, 8876.5, would give 8877 under 7.2 and 8876 under half-to-even rounding; neither is how totals are formed, because totals add rounded entries.
474	
475	### 16.5 Precedence of header lines
476	
477	A statement with `#dialect: lowmarsh` and `#date_order: dmy` is read with `dmy` dates whatever date order the `lowmarsh` dialect records, and with the dialect's delimiter, decimal mark and jurisdiction for the keys the header leaves out (3.4). `python -m ledger check FILE` prints the layout actually used.
478	
479	### 16.6 Negative amounts in output
480	
481	A month total of -50 cents is shown as `-0.50` in text, CSV, Markdown and HTML, and as `-50` in JSON. A total of -123456 cents is `-1,234.56` in text, Markdown and HTML and `-1234.56` in CSV (section 12).

Package layout\n\nThe package is split into sub-packages that depend on each other in one direction only, from the bottom of this list to the top:\n\n| Sub-package | Holds |\n|---|---|\n| `ledger.core` | `Money`, currency table, decimal parsing, rounding, id helpers |\n| `ledger.periods` | month keys, fiscal years, ISO weeks, business-day calendars, closed periods |\n| `ledger.parse` | header lines, dialects, amounts, dates, statement reading and writing, other file formats |\n| `ledger.fx` | rate files, the rate table, rate lookup, conversion, cross rates, revaluation |\n| `ledger.book` | entries, reversals and booking dates, chart of accounts, journal, transfers, splits, rules, audit |\n| `ledger.tax` | tax rules by jurisdiction and date, tax portions, returns, schedules |\n| `ledger.report` | monthly, tax, balance, trial balance, category, comparison and other reports |\n| `ledger.render` | text, CSV, Markdown, HTML and JSON output |\n| `ledger.cli` | the `python -m ledger` command line |\n\nModules whose names start with an underscore (`_currency_table`, `_dialect_table`, `_chart`, `_rule_table`, `_merchant_table`, `_holiday_table`) hold data tables. They are part of the package and are read at import time.\n\nThe base currency is the US dollar (`ledger.BASE_CURRENCY`). Every report value is an integer number of US cents.\n\n## 2. Statements\n\n### 2.1 File structure\n\nA statement is a text file in UTF-8. A leading byte order mark is ignored. The file has three parts, in this order:\n\n1. Header lines. Each starts with `#` and has the form `#key: value`. Keys are case-insensitive and are stored in lower case; values are stripped of surrounding spaces.\n2. The column line, which names the columns in the order the rows use them. Blank lines between the header and the column line are ignored.\n3. Rows. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored here too; such a `#` line is a comment, not a header.\n\nLine numbers in error messages are one-based and count every physical line of the file, including header lines and blank lines.\n\n### 2.2 Header keys\n\n| Key | Required | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `account` | yes | Name of the account the statement belongs to. Used as the report name. |\n| `currency` | yes | ISO 4217 code of the statement currency (case-insensitive). |\n| `dialect` | no | Name of a dialect from the dialect table (section 3). |\n| `delimiter` | no | Field separator (section 3.2). |\n| `decimal` | no | Decimal mark of amounts: `.` or `,`. |\n| `date_order` | no | `ymd`, `dmy` or `mdy` (section 5.1). |\n| `jurisdiction` | no | Tax jurisdiction code (section 10). Empty means the statement is not taxed. |\n| `fiscal_start` | no | Month number 1 to 12 in which the account's fiscal year starts (section 5.3). |\n| `opened` | no | Informational; not interpreted. |\n| `note` | no | Informational; not interpreted. |\n\nAn unknown key, a key that appears twice, or a missing required key is a `HeaderError`.\n\n### 2.3 Columns\n\nThe required columns are `id`, `date`, `description` and `amount`. The optional columns are `reverses`, `category` and `tax`. Column names are case-insensitive, and columns may appear in any order. An unknown column name, a repeated name or a missing required column is a `FormatError` on the column line.\n\nEvery row must have exactly as many fields as the column line. Fields are stripped of surrounding spaces. Quoting follows the usual CSV rules, so a field that contains the delimiter is written in double quotes.\n\n| Column | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `id` | Entry id, unique within the statement. Ids are compared exactly as written (case-sensitive). |\n| `date` | Posting date, in the statement's date order. |\n| `description` | Free text. |\n| `amount` | Signed amount in the statement currency (section 4). Positive amounts increase the account, negative amounts decrease it. |\n| `reverses` | Id of the entry this row cancels, or empty (section 8). |\n| `category` | Dotted category path, stored in lower case, or empty (section 9). |\n| `tax` | Tax code `S`, `R`, `Z` or `E`, stored in upper case, or empty (section 10). |\n\nAn empty id, an id used twice (`DuplicateEntry`) and an entry that reverses itself are errors.\n\n### 2.4 Other formats\n\n`ledger.parse.importers` reads two more formats into the same `Statement`: JSON lines (`.jsonl`) and fixed-width text (`.txt`). Both are converted to CSV text first, so every rule in this note applies to them unchanged. In both formats amounts are strings written in the statement's layout. A `delimiter` header key in these formats is ignored, because the converted text is always comma-delimited.\n\n### 2.5 Writing statements\n\n`ledger.parse.writer.write_statement` writes a statement so that it reads back to the same entries. It writes the dialect name when the statement has one and also every layout key explicitly, so the written file does not depend on the dialect table. Amounts are written without group separators and with a leading minus for negatives.\n\n## 3. Dialects and layout\n\n### 3.1 What a layout is\n\nThe layout of a statement is the set of four values that decide how its body is read: `delimiter`, `decimal`, `date_order` and `jurisdiction`. `Statement.layout` holds the layout a statement was read with, and `ledger check` prints it.\n\n### 3.2 Delimiter values\n\nA `delimiter` value is either a name (`comma`, `semicolon`, `pipe`, `tab`, case-insensitive) or a single character that is not a letter, a digit, a quote or `#`. A tab can only be given by name.\n\n### 3.3 Dialects\n\nA dialect records the layout one sender uses for all its statements, so that a header can name the sender (`#dialect: northgate`) instead of spelling each value out. Dialect names are case-insensitive. The table is in `ledger.parse._dialect_table`; an unknown name is `UnknownDialect`.\n\n### 3.4 Which value wins\n\nEach layout key takes its value from the first of these sources that has one:\n\n1. the statement's own header line for that key;\n2. the dialect named by the statement's `dialect` header;\n3. the base layout: delimiter `,`, decimal `.`, date order `ymd`, no jurisdiction.\n\nA header line therefore always wins over the dialect. This is what lets one sender's statement deviate from its usual layout (an export made with a different setting, or an account held in another jurisdiction) without a new dialect. A dialect only fills the keys the header leaves out.\n\nExample: the `northgate` dialect is semicolon-delimited with a `,` decimal mark, `dmy` dates and jurisdiction `ARD`. A statement with the header lines below is read with delimiter `,`, decimal `.`, `ymd` dates and jurisdiction `ARD`:\n\n    #account: cross-month\n    #currency: EUR\n    #dialect: northgate\n    #delimiter: comma\n    #decimal: .\n    #date_order: ymd\n\n### 3.5 Checks on a layout\n\n`decimal` must be `.` or `,`; `date_order` must be one of the three orders. The delimiter and the decimal mark must differ, except that a `,` delimiter with a `,` decimal mark is allowed because such amounts are quoted. Violations are `HeaderError`.\n\n### 3.6 Guessing\n\n`ledger.parse.sniff` guesses a layout from a file's body and `ledger check --guess` compares the guess with the layout the file is read with. The guess is advisory: reading always follows section 3.4, never the guess.\n\n## 4. Amounts\n\n### 4.1 Minor units\n\nAmounts are stored as integers in minor units of their currency. The number of minor-unit digits is the currency's exponent from `ledger.core._currency_table`: 2 for most currencies, 0 for currencies such as JPY or KRW, 3 for currencies such as KWD, BHD or TND. So `12.34` EUR is 1234, `1500` JPY is 1500 and `1.5` KWD is 1500.\n\n### 4.2 Accepted forms\n\nAn amount consists of, in order:\n\n- an optional sign: a leading `-` or `+`, or surrounding parentheses for a negative amount (`(7.25)` is -725). Spaces inside the parentheses are allowed. A sign inside parentheses, and unbalanced parentheses, are errors;\n- a whole part of digits, optionally with group separators;\n- optionally, the decimal mark followed by one or more digits, at most as many as the currency's exponent. Fewer digits are padded: `2450.5` is 245050 cents.\n\nThe decimal mark is the statement's `decimal` value. The group separator is `,` when the decimal mark is `.`, and `.` when the decimal mark is `,`. A space is also accepted as a group separator. Group separators may only appear in the whole part, and must split it into groups of three digits after a first group of one to three digits (`1,234,567` is fine, `12,34` is not).\n\nAnything else is a `FormatError`: an empty amount, more fraction digits than the exponent allows (`1.234` for EUR, `1.5` for JPY), a decimal mark without digits after it, more than one decimal mark, letters, or a bare sign.\n\n### 4.3 Display\n\nFormatting goes the other way (`ledger.core.money.format_amount`): the whole part, the decimal mark and exactly `exponent` fraction digits, with an optional group separator every three digits. A negative amount is written with a single leading minus sign before its digits and is otherwise written exactly like the positive amount of the same size: -50 cents is `-0.50`, -123456 cents is `-1,234.56` with `,` groups. Zero is never negative. Section 12 says which formats use which separators.\n\n## 5. Dates, months and fiscal periods\n\n### 5.1 Date orders\n\n| Order | Example | Separators |\n|---|---|---|\n| `ymd` | `2026-01-31` | `-` |\n| `dmy` | `31/01/2026`, `31.01.2026` | `/` or `.` |\n| `mdy` | `01/31/2026` | `/` |\n\nYears have four digits; day and month have one or two. A date that does not exist (`2026-02-30`) or does not match the order is a `FormatError`.\n\n### 5.2 Month keys\n\nA month key is `YYYY-MM`. Month keys sort correctly as strings. `iter_months(first, last)` includes both ends; `months_between(start, stop)` is half-open and excludes `stop`. A range written in a data file (rate files, section 6.1) always includes both of its end months.\n\n### 5.3 Fiscal years\n\nA fiscal year starts on the first day of the account's `fiscal_start` month (1 when absent) and is named after the calendar year in which it ends. With `fiscal_start` 4, April 2025 to March 2026 is FY2026. Quarters are numbered from the start of the fiscal year: with `fiscal_start` 4, January 2026 is in FY2026-Q4.\n\n### 5.4 Weeks and business days\n\nWeeks follow ISO 8601 (`ledger.periods.weeks`). A business day is a Monday to Friday that is not a public holiday of the statement's jurisdiction (`ledger.periods._holiday_table`); a statement without a jurisdiction only skips weekends. Business days are used by the aging report only.\n\n## 6. Exchange rates\n\n### 6.1 Rate files\n\nA rate file is a CSV file with the columns `currency`, `from`, `to` and `rate`, in that order. Lines starting with `#` and blank lines are ignored. Each row says that, in every month from `from` to `to` (both included), one major unit of `currency` was worth `rate` US dollars. A row whose `from` and `to` are the same month covers exactly that month.\n\nRules:\n\n- `rate` is a positive decimal written with digits and at most one `.`, with at most 8 decimal places. Exponent notation, signs and group separators are rejected.\n- `from` and `to` are month keys and `to` is not before `from`.\n- The base currency has no rows; a USD row is an error.\n- Two rows that cover the same currency and month are a `RateConflict`, whether they are in one file or in two files loaded together.\n\nThe table built from a rate file (`RateTable`) holds exactly the months the rows cover, one entry per currency and month.\n\n### 6.2 Which rate applies to a month\n\nThe rate for a currency in a month is chosen as follows:\n\n1. If the rate table lists the month, that rate is used.\n2. Otherwise the most recent earlier month that the table lists is used, provided it is at most three months before the month in question (`MAX_LOOKBACK`). The rate is then said to be carried from that month.\n3. Otherwise there is no rate, and `MissingRate` is raised.\n\nA later month's rate is never used, not even when it is closer than the nearest earlier one: it was not known at the time of the entry. Examples, with rates listed for January to March and for May:\n\n| Month | Rate used |\n|---|---|\n| March | March |\n| April | March (carried, one month back) |\n| May | May |\n| December of the year before | none: `MissingRate`, even though January is only one month later |\n\nWith rates listed only for January, April is carried from January (three months back) and May has no rate.\n\nThe base currency always has the rate 1 in every month.\n\n### 6.3 Cross rates\n\nThe cross rate from currency A to currency B in a month is rate(A) / rate(B), each chosen as in 6.2, rounded to 6 decimal places with the rule of section 7.2. Converting an amount between two non-base currencies goes through the base currency exactly, and only the result is rounded to whole minor units of B.\n\n## 7. Conversion and rounding\n\n### 7.1 Converting one entry\n\nAn amount of `m` minor units of a currency with exponent `e`, at rate `r`, is worth exactly `m * r * 10^(2 - e)` US cents. This value is computed with exact decimal arithmetic (Python `Decimal`), never with binary floats.\n\nEach entry is converted on its own and rounded to whole cents (7.2) before it is added to anything. Every total in every report (a month, a category, a tax code, a trial balance row, a report total) is a sum of rounded entry values. Totals are never rounded again, and an exact sum is never rounded as a whole. For example, two entries of 41.00 EUR at 1.0825 are each 4438.25 cents exactly; each rounds to 4438, and their month total is 8876, not the 8877 that rounding their exact sum 8876.5 would give.\n\n### 7.2 The rounding rule\n\nAll rounding in the package rounds to the nearest integer, and a value exactly halfway between two integers is rounded away from zero:\n\n| Exact value | Rounded |\n|---|---|\n| 216.5 | 217 |\n| -216.5 | -217 |\n| 2.5 | 3 |\n| 3.5 | 4 |\n| -0.5 | -1 |\n| 10.49 | 10 |\n\nThe same rule applies when rounding to decimal places (cross rates, percentages, statistics): 1.23455 to four places is 1.2346. Rounding half to even (\"banker's rounding\") is not used anywhere, because it does not match the rounding the senders use on their own statements.\n\n`ledger.core.rounding.round_half_away` implements this rule and every other module rounds through it (or through `round_to`, which uses the same rule).\n\n### 7.3 Allocation\n\n`allocate(total, weights)` splits an integer amount in proportion to weights with the largest remainder method; the shares always add up to the total. Remainders go one unit at a time to the largest fractional parts, earlier positions first on ties. Negative totals are allocated as their absolute value and negated.\n\n## 8. Reversals\n\n### 8.1 What a reversal is\n\nAn entry whose `reverses` column names another entry of the same statement cancels that entry. The entry it names is called the original.\n\n### 8.2 Checks\n\nA reversal must satisfy all of these, or `UnmatchedReversal` is raised:\n\n- the original exists in the same statement;\n- the original is itself a regular entry, not a reversal;\n- the reversal's amount is exactly the negated amount of the original;\n- the reversal is not dated before the original;\n- no other reversal already cancels the same original.\n\n### 8.3 Booking period and valuation\n\nA reversal does not create an event of its own in the reports; it undoes the original. Therefore:\n\n- it is booked in the period (month) of the original entry, not in the month in which it was posted;\n- it is valued as of the original entry's date: it is converted at the rate that applies to the original's month (section 6.2), and when it is taxed, the tax rule in force on the original's date applies (section 10.2).\n\nBoth dates come from the original. In `ledger.book.reversals`, a `Booking` carries a `period_date` and a `valuation_date`; for a regular entry both are its own date, and for a reversal both are the original's date. A matched pair therefore nets to exactly zero in every report, in every currency and for tax, even when the reversal is posted in a later month whose exchange rate or tax rate differs.\n\nExample: an entry of -150.40 EUR dated 20 January and its reversal dated 3 February both belong to January and are both converted at January's rate. The February report does not show either of them.\n\n### 8.4 Reversals elsewhere\n\nSplits (13.2) split a reversal with the same weights as its original, part by part. The audit (`ledger audit`) reports reversals posted more than 60 days after their original; this is informational only.\n\n## 9. Categories and accounts\n\n### 9.1 Resolution\n\nThe chart of accounts (`ledger.book._chart`) maps categories to account codes. A category is a dotted path such as `travel.rail.season`. An entry's category is resolved to the account of the longest listed prefix of its path: `travel.rail.night` uses the account of `travel.rail` when only that is listed, and `travel.bus` uses the account of `travel`. Categories are compared in lower case.\n\nAn empty category goes to the suspense account `9990`. A non-empty category with no listed prefix, or with an empty segment (`travel..rail`), is `UnknownCategory`.\n\n### 9.2 Suggestions and rules\n\n`ledger suggest` proposes categories for entries without one, from the merchant table. Suggestions are never applied by the reports. A rules file (`ledger.book.rules`) can assign categories to uncategorized entries before booking, when a caller applies it explicitly; reading a statement never applies rules.\n\n## 10. Tax\n\n### 10.1 Codes and jurisdictions\n\nTax codes are `S` (standard), `R` (reduced), `Z` (zero rated) and `E` (exempt). Each jurisdiction in `ledger.tax._rule_table` has, per code, a list of rules: a date from which a rate applies, and the rate. Rates in the table are written as fractions (`0.095`) or percentages (`9.5%`).\n\nA statement is taxed in its layout's jurisdiction. An entry with a tax code in a statement without a jurisdiction, an unknown jurisdiction, an unknown code, or a date before the code's first rule is `UnknownTaxCode`. Entries without a tax code are not part of tax reports.\n\n### 10.2 Which rule applies\n\nThe rule that applies on a day is the rule of the entry's code with the latest effective date that is on or before that day. A rule takes effect on its effective date itself: a rate that applies from 1 March 2026 applies to an entry valued on 1 March 2026, and the previous rate applies to an entry valued on 28 February 2026.\n\nThe day is the entry's valuation date (section 8.3): its own date for a regular entry, the original's date for a reversal.\n\n### 10.3 Tax portion\n\nStatement amounts include tax. For an entry, the gross amount G is its converted and rounded value in US cents (section 7.1). With rate r, the tax portion is G * r / (1 + r) rounded with the rule of 7.2, and the net amount is G minus the tax portion. Tax portions are computed per entry and then added up; they are never computed from a total.\n\nBecause the rounding rule is symmetric, the tax of a reversal is exactly the negated tax of its original.\n\n### 10.4 Returns and schedules\n\nA quarterly return (`ledger return`) adds the per-entry tax lines of one jurisdiction's statements by calendar quarter of their valuation dates. `ledger schedule` prints a jurisdiction's rules; each rule's \"until\" date is the effective date of the next rule of the same code, and the rule no longer applies on that date.\n\n## 11. Reports\n\n### 11.1 Monthly report\n\n`build_monthly` returns:\n\n    {\"account\": \"...\", \"currency\": \"EUR\", \"base\": \"USD\",\n     \"months\": {\"2026-01\": -12345, ...}, \"total\": -12345}\n\n`months` holds, for each booking period that has at least one entry, the sum of the rounded values of the entries booked in it (sections 7.1 and 8.3), in calendar order. A month whose entries cancel out is listed with 0. `total` is the sum of the month values.\n\n### 11.2 Tax report\n\n`build_vat` returns, per tax code used by the statement, the sums of the per-entry gross, net and tax amounts (section 10.3), plus `total_tax`, the sum of the tax amounts. Codes are listed in alphabetical order. A statement without taxed entries has an empty `codes` mapping.\n\n### 11.3 Balances, summaries and comparisons\n\n- Balances list every month from the first to the last month of a monthly report, months without entries included, with the movement and the closing balance.\n- Fiscal summaries add month values by fiscal quarter and fiscal year (section 5.3).\n- Month-over-month and year-over-year comparisons give percentages rounded to one decimal with the rule of 7.2, written with a sign (`+12.5%`). A change from zero is `new`.\n\n### 11.4 Trial balance and account matrix\n\nThe trial balance and the account-by-month matrix are built from journal postings. A posting is one entry, booked and valued as in sections 7 and 8, assigned to the account of its category. An account's net is the sum of its postings; a positive net is shown as a debit and a negative net, as a positive number, as a credit.\n\n### 11.5 Other reports\n\n- Aging lists open receivables (positive regular entries in a `receivable` account that no reversal cancels) by business days outstanding, in buckets 0-20, 21-40, 41-60 and 61+. Amounts stay in the statement currency.\n- Revaluation compares, at each month end, the book value (sum of posted rounded values) with the running balance converted once at that month's rate.\n- Reconciliation compares sender-reported closing balances with the sum of entries by posting date. It deliberately ignores booking periods, because the sender does not know them.\n- Budgets compare planned and actual account totals by month.\n\n## 12. Rendering\n\nAll renderers take the report dicts of section 11 and show amounts in major units of US dollars with two decimals.\n\n| Format | Decimal mark | Group separator | Negative amounts | Example |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| text | `.` | `,` | leading minus | `-1,234.56` |\n| CSV | `.` | none | leading minus | `-1234.56` |\n| Markdown | `.` | `,` | leading minus | `-1,234.56` |\n| HTML | `.` | `,` | leading minus, cell class `neg` | `-1,234.56` |\n| JSON | not applicable | not applicable | integer cents | `-123456` |\n\nAll of them use `ledger.core.money.format_amount`, whose output is defined in section 4.3; a renderer never formats amounts on its own. Small negative amounts keep their sign: -50 cents is `-0.50` in text, CSV, Markdown and HTML alike.\n\nThe accounting style (`format_accounting`) puts negative amounts in parentheses. It is only used where a caller asks for it explicitly; no report format uses it.\n\nText output: a title line, then a table whose columns are separated by two spaces, text left-aligned and amounts right-aligned, with trailing spaces removed from every line. The monthly report's last row is `total`.\n\nCSV output: a header row, then one row per line of the report, lines ending with `\\n`, fields quoted only when needed.\n\nMarkdown output: a `###` title, a blank line, and a pipe table whose amount columns are right-aligned (`---:`); the total row's label is bold.\n\nJSON output: keys sorted, two-space indentation, a final newline.\n\n## 13. Auxiliary files\n\n### 13.1 Budgets\n\nCSV with columns `account`, `month`, `amount`; amounts in US dollars with a `.` decimal mark, negative for spending. One line per account and month.\n\n### 13.2 Splits\n\nCSV with columns `id`, `category`, `weight`. An entry named in the file is replaced by one part per line, sharing its amount with `allocate` (section 7.3). Part ids get the suffix `/1`, `/2`, ... in file order.\n\n### 13.3 Closing files\n\nOne month key per line; `#` starts a comment. `late_entries` lists the entries booked into a closed month although they were posted after that month ended (for instance a reversal posted in February of an entry from a closed January).\n\n### 13.4 Balance files\n\nCSV with columns `month` and `closing`; amounts in the statement currency with a `.` decimal mark.\n\n### 13.5 Workspace file\n\n`ledger.toml` may set `[ledger] rates`, `statements` and `pattern`, and `[report] format`. Unknown sections or keys are errors.\n\n## 14. Command line\n\n`python -m ledger <command>` runs from the workspace directory. Rates come from `--rates`, else from the `LEDGER_RATES` environment variable, else from `data/rates.csv` under the current directory. Output goes to standard output; errors go to standard error as `ledger: <ErrorType>: <message>` with exit status 2. `python -m ledger --help` and `python -m ledger <command> --help` list the commands and options.\n\n### 14.1 Reports of one statement\n\n| Command | Output |\n|---|---|\n| `report STATEMENT [--format F] [--detail]` | Monthly report (11.1). With `--detail`, one CSV line per entry: id, posting date, booking period, the month whose rate was used, and the value in US dollars. |\n| `vat STATEMENT [--format F]` | Tax report (11.2). |\n| `balances STATEMENT [--format F]` | Running balances (11.3). |\n| `summary STATEMENT [--format F]` | Fiscal quarters and years (11.3). |\n| `explain STATEMENT ID` | How one entry is read, booked, valued and taxed, one stage per line. |\n| `revalue STATEMENT` | Month-end revaluation (11.5), as JSON. |\n| `aging STATEMENT DATE` | Open receivables on DATE (11.5). |\n| `audit STATEMENT` | Findings worth a second look; they never stop a report. |\n| `suggest STATEMENT` | Category suggestions for uncategorized entries (9.2). |\n| `outlook STATEMENT [--months N]` | Recurring payments projected forward, in the statement currency. |\n\n`--format` is one of `text`, `csv`, `markdown` and `json` (section 12); `text` when absent.\n\n### 14.2 Several statements\n\n| Command | Output |\n|---|---|\n| `trial STATEMENT... [--period MONTH]` | Trial balance (11.4), optionally for one booking period. |\n| `matrix STATEMENT...` | Account-by-month matrix (11.4), as JSON. |\n| `transfers STATEMENT...` | Pairs of cash entries in different statements that cancel within a tolerance and lie at most three days apart. |\n| `return STATEMENT...` | Quarterly tax return of one jurisdiction (10.4), as JSON. |\n| `export STATEMENT...` | Postings as plain-text double-entry transactions. |\n| `budget BUDGET STATEMENT...` | Budget against actual (13.1), as CSV. |\n| `overview STATEMENT...` | One line per statement: currency, dialect, entries, reversals, date range. |\n\n### 14.3 Files and tables\n\n| Command | Output |\n|---|---|\n| `check STATEMENT... [--guess]` | One line per statement: `ok` with the layout it was read with, or `FAIL` with the first problem. Exit status 1 when any statement fails. With `--guess`, also compares each file's body with that layout (3.6). |\n| `validate STATEMENT` | Every row-level problem of a statement, not only the first. |\n| `diff OLD NEW` | Entries added, removed or changed between two versions of a statement, and layout changes. |\n| `rate CURRENCY MONTH` | The rate that applies (6.2) and the month it comes from. |\n| `rates` | Per currency: listed range, missing months, low, high, mean and spread of the rates. |\n| `dialects [NAME]` | The dialect table, or one dialect's layout. |\n| `schedule JURISDICTION` | Every tax rule of a jurisdiction with the date it ends (10.4). |\n\n## 15. Errors\n\nEvery error the package raises on purpose is a `LedgerError`. `FormatError` (and its subclass `HeaderError`) carry the file and one-based line when they come from a file, and show them as `path line N: message`. Errors are raised, never logged and skipped: a statement either reads completely or not at all.\n\n## 16. Worked examples\n\nThe examples use these rates: EUR 1.0825 for January to March 2026 (one row), EUR 1.0910 for May and June 2026, and nothing for April.\n\n### 16.1 One entry from file to report\n\nA row `b3,2026-02-02,Rail pass,-84,,travel.rail.season,R` in a EUR statement with jurisdiction ARD:\n\n1. Amount: `-84` has no fraction, so it is -8400 minor units (4.2).\n2. Booking: a regular entry, so period and valuation date are its own date, 2 February 2026 (8.3).\n3. Rate: February is listed, rate 1.0825 (6.2).\n4. Conversion: -8400 * 1.0825 = -9093.0000 cents exactly, -9093 after rounding (7.1).\n5.
